existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Treats political thinking as historical activity within available languages and distinguishes this inquiry from extracting only systematically coherent philosophy (1962; reformulated 1996).
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Selected 1962 reprint pp. 3–4, 9–11 and 1996 pp. 47–50 read. This is an individual contribution within the contextual field, not an exclusive founding claim. The existing collective field-to-intellectual-history arrow, also naming Skinner and Brett, is preserved.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Asks whether an alphabetical history of concepts can reconstruct the complexity of political languages and avoid projecting the historian’s categories onto earlier actors (published 1996).
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Pocock, Concepts and Discourses, pp. 47–55, especially pp. 50–55. He explicitly cannot read German and responds to Richter’s presentation of the lexicon. He welcomes a complementary conceptual history and does not dismiss Koselleck’s project or claim first-hand inspection of all its articles. The distinction is an acknowledged methodological challenge, not an assertion that Cambridge and conceptual history are mutually exclusive schools.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Singles out Skinner’s search for the modern concept of the state as exposed to the risk of imposing later categories on language users who did not employ those terms (published 1996).
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Pocock pp. 54–55 and p. 55 n. 2 explicitly name The Foundations of Modern Political Thought, volume II’s conclusion (1978), and the essay The State. This specific criticism coexists with substantial sympathy for Skinner’s general methodological contention and intellectual collaboration. The cited books/essay were not newly read or independently judged here.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Answers Pocock’s objections by treating discourse and conceptual history as interdependent and defending alphabetical organization as a way to leave historical transformation open to investigation (published 1996).
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Koselleck’s own response pp. 62–66, especially pp. 64–66, read. He accepts the uniqueness of situated speech acts but argues that later reception and reuse make conceptual history necessary. He rejects a general incompatibility of methods; this does not mean that Pocock himself asserted such a simple opposition. This is a qualified methodological answer to specific questions, not a complete rebuttal of Pocock’s scholarship.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Pagden uses Pocock’s account of political languages as distinguishable language-games to explain how historians reconstruct an argument’s vocabularies, conventions and intelligibility.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Pagden’s own opening discussion explicitly names and uses Pocock’s formulation. The publisher’s substantive opening excerpt was read; the complete 1987 introduction and Pocock’s chapter were not freshly read. This is a particular methodological resource, not influence inferred from the editorship or the whole Cambridge school. The print contribution is 1987; 2009 is the online publication date.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Bailyn identifies Pocock’s research among the resources used to reconstruct the British opposition traditions in revolutionary American thought.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The foreword reproduced in the 1992 enlarged edition, printed xii, explicitly places Pocock with other British political-thought researchers. Robbins, Gough, Laslett, Weston and other named scholars retain their distinct credit; no sole-source or general Cambridge-school lineage is asserted. The original 1967 copy and Pocock’s cited works were not collated or freshly read.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: As Soll reconstructs, Rodgers challenges the reach of Pocock’s early republican-language paradigm and calls for political, social and cultural contexts beyond it.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Soll 2010, printed 22 and notes 4–6, reconstructs Rodgers 1992, 37–38, and retains Rodgers’s acknowledgment of the republican debate’s contribution to constitutional history. The claim is limited to the strong early paradigm, not all of Pocock’s changing work. Soll’s later criticisms of Skinner/Tuck are his own and are not assigned to Rodgers. Original 1992 essay and Pocock’s books were not freshly read.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Armitage credits Pocock among his lasting intellectual inspirations during his Princeton fellowship.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2000 acknowledgment expressly distinguishes Princeton inspiration from later Cambridge questions and examination. Elliott, Lake, Quint and the other Princeton colleague retain plural credit. This narrow self-reported formative debt identifies no particular doctrine, book or sole supervisor; their works remain unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Morgan uses Pocock’s reconstruction of republican political ideas to explain the connection between property, independence and liberty in Jefferson’s outlook.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 1972, 8/n6 and 9/n9, uses Pocock’s 1965 Machiavelli/Harrington study alongside Caroline Robbins, and in the colonial political comparison with Michael Zuckerman/Robert Weir. These plural resources substantiate one part of the American-paradox argument, not a claim that Pocock supplied its whole slavery mechanism. Original 1965 essay and the other cited works remain unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Wood borrows Pocock’s formulation of a Namierian history of ideas to characterize Bailyn’s analysis of revolutionary thought.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 1966 applies a specifically credited analytical formulation across the 21–22 page break, n41 citing Pocock’s 1965 article p550. This is a small conceptual resource, not evidence that Wood adopted the whole later republican synthesis or a claim that Pocock coined every underlying idea. Pocock’s original article unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Wood questions the explanatory limits and fixed republican categories of Pocock’s synthesis.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own1985 review of Diggins distinguishes Pocock’s synthesis from Diggins’s polemic. Wood questions its account of liberal America and objects to rigid categories, while recognizing its impact. He also reports Pocock’s self-qualification. Full Pocock and Diggins books unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Lears finds Pocock’s linguistic history helpful but too intellectualist for the cultural-hegemony inquiry he outlines.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own qualified note concerns Politics, Language, and Time1971,3–41; it accompanies proposals to study broader cultural texts and symbolic practices. No blanket rejection of intellectual history or a claim to have read Pocock’s entire book.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Colley takes up Pocock’s expanded British-history agenda and his account of Britain’s post-imperial relation to Europe.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Primary pp.312–313 explains both the Four Nations gains and Pocock’s wider white-empire programme; p. 328 explicitly uses his observation that Britain can no longer control or avoid Europe,n. 53. Colley’s criticism of a narrowed Four Nations reception is not assigned to Pocock himself: she stresses that his original programme was geographically wider. UnderlyingPocock 1975/1982 articles unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Trouillot includes Pocock among contributors whose leads, comments or documents made a substantive difference to Silencing the Past.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own xviii–xix collective acknowledgment describes several possible forms of contribution and explicitly says results were not always intended by contributors. It does not assign a particular comment to Pocock, certify whole-manuscript reading, establish agreement or claim formal training.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: renews study of political argument and action
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages renew political-intellectual questions; their approaches are not identical. Skinner’s selected 1969 pages distinguish causal conditions from intended interventions. Pocock’s methodological excerpt asks about actual levels of thinking, while the 1975 introduction selects republican fragility and a proposed Atlantic continuation; the latter’s full transmission argument is not independently verified here.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Skinner explicitly credits the Investigations in asking about historical language use
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Interview answer 6 recalls reading and discussing the work, connecting it to purposeful discourse and public intentions. This retrospective evidence concerns Skinner’s pre-2000 practice; it does not establish one philosophy shared by Pocock or all contextual historians. The 1969 article p. 37 directly cites Investigations §§43 and 79, adding contemporary primary evidence to the retrospective interview. Endpoint review 2026-10-24: the retained statement names this promoted individual; only its endpoint is repaired. Prior sources, wording and reading qualifications remain. See the individual entry and research packet for the fresh reading scope.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Stone identifies contextual histories of political thought as a resource
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Page 14 names Pocock, Skinner and Bailyn in discussing changed meanings. His general assessment is not proof of one shared method.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Skinner, Pocock and Brett: contextual inquiries
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Named approaches contribute to a wider field without defining it or subsuming every intellectual historian.
named_group_routes_inspected.map_label: Skinner, Pocock and Brett: contextual inquiries

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Canada and the British World: imperial history from the settler colonies
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Buckner (1993, abstract) argues that historians of the second British Empire neglect the colonies of settlement and Pocock's "Greater Britain", and that historians of the settler colonies share the blame; Canada and the British World (2006) surveys Canadian history "through a British lens" while eschewing nostalgia. The atlas has no separate imperial-history entry; nationaltradition (national and imperial narratives) is the nearest. Comparison, scoped to the British World strand.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Makes the historically possible intervention, rather than a timeless doctrine, central to interpreting political texts; recalls that public uses and intentions guided his practice (1969; retrospective interview 2002).
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: 1969 pp. 37–38, 50–52 and 2002 answers 1/6 reread, with the earlier wider reading scope retained. This is his individual methodological contribution to the contextual field. The reception arrows for Wittgenstein and Collingwood keep their old IDs; aggregate edges also naming Dunn, Pocock and Brett are not reassigned to him.
